summary: object distance (g) is what the Lens magnification calculator works out, and it gets there from the focal distance, the sensor distance and the extension tube. It is built for whatever you happen to be working on. The unit chips sit next to the boxes, which is where most hand-calculation mistakes start.

sections.title: How does the Lens magnification calculator work?
sections.html:
The Lens magnification calculator takes the values in the form, applies the relationship described below and reports object distance (g) in the results panel.

Working from the top of the form: you type in the focal distance (f), the sensor distance (h) and the extension tube.

The arithmetic runs locally each time an input changes. The page knows which values you have given it and which it still has to derive, so the results panel is never stale.

Because the equation can be rearranged for each of its variables, the page also runs backwards. Leave the box you want to know empty, fill in the rest, and it solves for the missing one instead. That is useful when you know the answer you need rather than the inputs you have.

sections.title: The formula behind the Lens magnification calculator
sections.html:
The page rests on a handful of relationships. Each one can be rearranged for any of its variables, which is what makes the calculator work in both directions:

Object distance (g)=(1 ÷ 2) × focus distance (d) + R
R=(1 ÷ 2) × focus distance (d) − sensor distance (h)
R=(1 ÷ 2) × the square root of (focus distance (d) × (-4 × focal distance (f) + focus distance (d)))
Magnification=((extension tube + sensor distance (h)) ÷ object distance (g))

Read it as an ordinary equation. Where a word appears instead of a letter, it is the label of one of the boxes in the form; where a function appears, it is the usual mathematical meaning of that function.

sections.title: What is a worked example?
sections.html:
Suppose Focus distance (d) = 30 m, Extension tube = 0 mm and R = 30 m. Working through the relationship above gives Focal distance (f) = -22.5 mm, Magnification = -0.3333, Object distance (g) = 45 m and Sensor distance (h) = -15 m.

Read it as a template. Every number above can be replaced with one of yours; only the relationship between them is fixed.

  1. Enter the values listed above, matching the units each box asks for.
  2. Read off the result. Any field you leave empty is the one the calculator solves for.
  3. Sanity-check the number against the relationship: Focal distance (f) = -22.5 mm, Magnification = -0.3333, Object distance (g) = 45 m and Sensor distance (h) = -15 m should be roughly the size you expected from Focus distance (d) = 30 m and Extension tube = 0 mm.

sections.title: How are units and precision handled?
sections.html:
Every quantity with units carries a chip beside its box. Switching the chip does not change what you know, only how it is written: values are converted to a common internal base, the arithmetic happens there, and the answer is converted back for display. Mixing metres with feet in one calculation is therefore safe.

Results are rounded for display but computed at full precision, so chaining one result into the next does not accumulate error. Very large and very small numbers switch to scientific notation rather than printing a run of zeros.

sections.title: When should you use it?
sections.html:
The Lens magnification calculator earns its place in the middle of a task, not instead of one. It is most useful when:

  • Testing how sensitive an answer is to one input
  • Turning a rough idea into a number you can act on
  • Checking a figure someone else quoted
  • Any time the same 3 figures keep coming back — the focal distance, the sensor distance and the extension tube — and you would rather not repeat the arithmetic by hand each time.

sections.title: How do you get a reliable answer?
sections.html:
• Round only at the end. The calculator carries full precision internally, so re-entering a value you already rounded is the fastest way to introduce drift.
  • Write the answer down with its unit. A bare number copied into a report later is exactly where units get lost.
  • Leave the field you want solved for empty rather than guessing at it. Filling every box tells the calculator you already know the answer.
  • Compare two scenarios by changing the input that actually differs between them, and keep the rest fixed, so the difference you see is the difference you meant to test.

sections.title: What else is worth knowing?
sections.html: • Filling in more than one box is fine. The most recently edited field is the one treated as known, so you can switch direction without reloading.

faq.q: What does the Lens magnification calculator work out?
faq.a: It returns object distance (g), derived from the focal distance, the sensor distance and the extension tube. Every field in the form feeds the same relationship: press Calculate once and changing any of them updates the result immediately, with no page reload.

faq.q: What do I need to enter to use the Lens magnification calculator?
faq.a: The form asks for the focal distance, the sensor distance and the extension tube, which is 3 fields in total. Each one is labelled with what it means and, where relevant, the unit it expects. Anything you leave blank is treated as the value to solve for.

faq.q: Can I enter focus distance (d) in a different unit?
faq.a: Yes. Focus distance (d) opens in meters and the chip beside it offers 34 units. The number you typed keeps its magnitude and only its label changes; the calculation itself happens in a common base unit, so mixing systems in one form is safe.
Yes. Each variable in the relationship can be the one being solved for: fill in the answer you are aiming at, leave the field you want empty, and the calculator inverts the equation for you.

With the values the page starts from, the calculator reports Focal distance (f) = -22.5 mm. Treat that as a reference point rather than a recommendation: it exists so you can tell at a glance whether your own inputs are on the same scale.

faq.q: Is the Lens magnification calculator free to use?
faq.a: Yes — no account, no sign-up and no limit on how many times you run it. The arithmetic happens in your browser, so the values you type are not sent anywhere.
